title: Number of Segments in a String
description:
# Number of Segments in a String

Given a string `s`, return the number of segments in `s`.

A segment is a group of consecutive non-space characters separated by ordinary spaces `' '` or string boundaries. Letters, digits, and punctuation without intervening spaces belong to the same segment.

Do not count empty runs created by leading spaces, trailing spaces, or multiple consecutive spaces.

## Example 1:

**Input:** s = "Hello, my name is John"
**Output:** 5
**Explanation:** The five segments are `"Hello,"`, `"my"`, `"name"`, `"is"`, and `"John"`.

## Example 2:

**Input:** s = "Hello"
**Output:** 1
**Explanation:** A single non-space run is one segment.

## Example 3:

**Input:** s = "  leading and trailing  "
**Output:** 3
**Explanation:** Leading and trailing spaces do not create extra segments.

## Constraints:

* `0 <= s.length <= 300`
* `s` consists of lowercase and uppercase English letters, digits, spaces, or one of the following punctuation characters: `!@#$%^&*()_+-=',.:`.
* The only whitespace character in `s` is the ordinary space character `' '`.

solutions.name: Segment-Start Boundary Count
solutions.description:
## Approach

Scan from left to right and count every character that starts a segment. A character starts a segment when it is not a space and either it is at index `0` or the previous character is a space.

## Key Insight

The definition of a segment is a maximal non-space run, so every segment has exactly one first character. Counting those first characters avoids building substrings and naturally ignores repeated spaces.

## Complexity Analysis

- Time Complexity: O(n)
- Space Complexity: O(1)

solutions.name: Segment-End Boundary Count
solutions.description:
## Approach

Scan the string and count the last character of each segment. A non-space character ends a segment when it is at the last index or the next character is a space.

## Key Insight

Counting segment ends is the dual view of counting starts. It is useful for teaching that a maximal run can be recognized from either boundary, as long as consecutive spaces are not counted as runs.

## Complexity Analysis

- Time Complexity: O(n)
- Space Complexity: O(1)

solutions.name: In-Segment State Machine
solutions.description:
## Approach

Maintain a boolean `inside` that records whether the scan is currently inside a segment. Spaces move the state outside; a non-space character seen while outside starts a new segment.

## Key Insight

The input is a stream of separators and segment characters. A new segment is exactly the transition from outside to inside, which makes leading, trailing, and repeated spaces explicit.

## Complexity Analysis

- Time Complexity: O(n)
- Space Complexity: O(1)

solutions.name: Two-Phase Skip Runs
solutions.description:
## Approach

Use one index as a manual tokenizer. First skip a run of spaces; if the scan has not reached the end, count one segment and then skip the following run of non-space characters.

## Key Insight

This route mirrors how a parser consumes tokens: separators are discarded, then one whole token is consumed. Each character is advanced over at most once.

## Complexity Analysis

- Time Complexity: O(n)
- Space Complexity: O(1)

solutions.name: Trim and Split Baseline
solutions.description:
## Approach

Trim spaces from both ends. If the remaining string is empty, return `0`; otherwise split on one or more spaces and return the number of produced tokens.

## Key Insight

Library splitting is concise and easy to compare against the hand-written scans, but it allocates substrings and an array, so it is a baseline rather than the preferred constant-space solution.

## Complexity Analysis

- Time Complexity: O(n)
- Space Complexity: O(n)

tests.description: The canonical example has five non-space runs.
A single word is one segment.
The empty string has no segments.
Spaces alone do not create segments.
Multiple spaces between words still separate only three segments.
Leading and trailing spaces are ignored.
Punctuation is part of a segment when no spaces split it.
A one-character segment can be surrounded by spaces.
Single spaces between one-letter segments should count each segment.
Punctuation and digits are segment characters; spaces are the only separators.
Several internal space runs should not create empty segments.
Allowed punctuation characters form ordinary segments.
